paragraphs: Teaching a robot through reinforcement learning requires specifying what counts as success. For complex tasks, that can mean combining several objectives with safety constraints inside one reward function. The paper addresses the difficulty of translating such requirements into rewards that also give a learning algorithm useful guidance.

The proposed approach introduces a language for describing complex control tasks. An accompanying compiler converts those descriptions into reward functions and automatically performs reward shaping. Shaping supplies additional learning guidance, a step that users would otherwise often carry out manually. The language therefore connects a task description to both its reward representation and the guidance used during learning.

The authors implement this approach in SPECTRL and report that it outperforms several leading baselines. The contribution combines a way to express tasks with an automated route from specifications to learning signals. This matters because specifying the intended behavior and making it learnable are closely connected practical problems in reinforcement learning.
neurips-2019-a-composable-specification-.tldr: SPECTRL compiles descriptions of complex control tasks into reward functions and automatically shapes rewards to support reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate symmetric properties of a probability distribution from independent samples drawn from that same distribution. Such properties concern the distribution without depending on the particular names assigned to its outcomes. The central question is when simple estimation from observed frequencies is adequate and when more elaborate methods are needed.

The authors identify easy and difficult regions for a broad class of these properties. Empirical estimation works in the easy region. In the difficult region, their framework approximately computes a profile maximum likelihood distribution, using what they call pseudo PML distributions. This division gives the more complex estimator a specific role where empirical estimation is insufficient.

For many properties, the resulting framework achieves optimal sample complexity over a broader parameter regime than earlier universal PML approaches. This means its sample requirements meet the relevant optimum in those settings. The authors also describe the resulting algorithms as more practical, combining stronger statistical coverage with a more usable estimation approach.
neurips-2019-a-general-framework-for-sym.tldr: Separating easy and difficult estimation regions yields a practical PML-based framework with optimal sample complexity for many symmetric properties.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to use experience across tasks to improve learning on other tasks. Its usefulness depends on what those tasks share. This paper develops a theoretical framework that connects formal descriptions of task similarity with online convex optimization and sequential prediction, giving practical meta-learning methods a common basis for analysis and design.

A central feature is that the framework allows task similarity itself to be learned adaptively. The theory provides sharper bounds on transfer risk in statistical learning-to-learn. It also supports derivations of average-case regret bounds for efficient algorithms when the task environment changes over time or when tasks have a shared geometric structure.

The authors use these theoretical results to modify several popular meta-learning algorithms. They report improvements during training and at meta-test time on standard few-shot and federated learning problems. The contribution thus connects guarantees about transferring knowledge across tasks to concrete algorithm changes, including settings where the relationship among tasks cannot simply be treated as fixed.
neurips-2019-adaptive-gradient-based-met.tldr: An adaptive theory of task similarity guides changes to meta-learning algorithms that improve reported few-shot and federated learning performance.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means using familiar pieces of knowledge in new combinations. Learning a new action, for example, should make it possible to understand a request to repeat that action. The paper addresses the difficulty sequence-to-sequence neural networks have with this ability, particularly when combining newly learned concepts with concepts they already know.

The proposed method trains memory-augmented networks through meta sequence-to-sequence learning. Models encounter a series of sequence-to-sequence problems and learn compositional skills that can support solving new problems. This makes the training experience itself span multiple problems, so that learning how to handle new combinations becomes part of what the model acquires.

The reported results show that this approach solves several SCAN tests of compositional learning and can learn to apply implicit rules to variables. These findings support the possibility of learning reusable compositional behavior through this training setup. The stated success concerns several tests and rule-application capabilities, rather than a claim that all forms of compositional generalization have been solved.
neurips-2019-compositional-generalizatio.tldr: Training memory-augmented networks across sequence-to-sequence problems enables success on several tests of compositional generalization.

paragraphs: A standard convolutional layer applies the same learned kernels to every example. This paper questions whether that shared computation is the best way to expand a network's capacity while keeping prediction efficient. Its proposed layer, CondConv, learns convolutional kernels that are specialized for each example.

Replacing ordinary convolutions with these conditionally parameterized layers lets the network increase its size and capacity while maintaining efficient inference. The important distinction is between how much capacity a model contains and the computation needed to process an individual input. CondConv uses example-specific kernels to improve that relationship within existing convolutional architectures.

The authors demonstrate better trade-offs between performance and inference cost across several architectures on classification and detection tasks. For ImageNet classification, CondConv applied to EfficientNet-B0 reaches 78.3% accuracy using 413 million multiply-adds, which the paper reports as state-of-the-art performance. These results support conditional convolution as a practical way to scale capacity under computational constraints in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-condconv-conditionally-para.tldr: CondConv learns example-specific convolutional kernels to increase network capacity while improving the accuracy–inference cost trade-off.

paragraphs: Video compression must represent a sequence compactly while preserving useful visual detail. This paper proposes an end-to-end learned approach built around a generative model for sequential data. It combines sequential variational autoencoders with techniques from neural image compression to address the temporal structure of video.

The system jointly learns several parts of the compression process. It transforms the original sequence into a lower-dimensional representation, discretizes that representation, and entropy codes it using predictions from the sequential model. Learning these components together connects the representation being stored with the model used to encode it efficiently.

Evaluations examine the trade-off between compressed size and reconstruction distortion on small videos from public datasets with different levels of complexity and diversity. Training on generic video content produces competitive results, while training on specialized content achieves extreme compression. The findings distinguish a broadly trained compressor from one adapted to particular content: the strongest compression claim is tied to that specialized training setting.
neurips-2019-deep-generative-video-compr.tldr: A sequential generative model jointly learns video representation and coding, with competitive generic performance and extreme compression on specialized content.

paragraphs: Standard deep learning relies on weight transport: weights used in the forward computation must also be available to a feedback pathway. The paper argues that this requirement is probably incompatible with biological learning. Random feedback weights avoid transporting weights, but the existing feedback alignment approach performs poorly on difficult visual recognition tasks.

The authors introduce two mechanisms that allow the feedback pathway to learn suitable weights. One is a neural circuit called a weight mirror; the other modifies an earlier algorithm by Kolen and Pollack. Both are described as learning feedback weights quickly and accurately in large networks without weight transport or complicated wiring.

On ImageNet, the mechanisms outperform feedback alignment and the newer sign-symmetry method, while nearly matching standard backpropagation. The result narrows the performance gap between backpropagation and approaches that avoid its weight-transport requirement. It provides evidence for effective alternative learning mechanisms on a challenging recognition task, while the motivation about biological feasibility remains a qualified argument.
neurips-2019-deep-learning-without-weigh.tldr: Two mechanisms learn effective feedback weights without weight transport and nearly match backpropagation on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Combining multiple kinds of input requires modeling relationships among their features. The paper argues that existing tensor-based fusion approaches restrict those relationships by considering only bilinear or trilinear interactions. It also identifies a second problem: combining all features at once can overlook local correlations that matter for prediction.

The proposed polynomial tensor pooling block captures higher-order moments when integrating multimodal features, followed by a tensorized fully connected layer. The authors then stack these blocks into a hierarchical polynomial fusion network. This hierarchy progressively carries local correlations into global relationships, making the organization of feature interactions part of the model's design.

The paper establishes exponential growth in expressive capacity with the number of layers through an equivalence to very deep convolutional arithmetic circuits. This is a claim about representational power, rather than an exponential improvement in accuracy. Experiments report state-of-the-art predictive performance, supporting the use of both higher-order interactions and hierarchical fusion in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-deep-multimodal-multilinear.tldr: Hierarchical polynomial pooling combines higher-order multimodal interactions with local-to-global fusion and reports state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Selecting a useful subset often requires balancing the quality of individual items against diversity across the whole set. Determinantal point processes provide a way to do this, but their sampling procedures can be expensive. The paper targets that computational burden by learning to generate samples with DPP-like properties.

DppNets are deep generative models designed to work with arbitrary ground sets. Their central mechanism is inhibitive attention, built using transformer networks to capture dissimilarity between feature vectors. The authors provide theoretical support that the approximation preserves guarantees associated with inhibition or dissimilarity, the behavior that makes DPPs useful for diverse selection.

Across multiple datasets, DppNet produces samples orders of magnitude faster than competing DPP sampling approaches. Those samples have high likelihood, and downstream performance matches DPPs in the reported experiments. Together, these findings suggest that a learned approximation can retain useful selection behavior while substantially reducing sampling cost. The model produces DPP-like samples rather than claiming exact DPP sampling.
neurips-2019-dppnet-approximating-determ.tldr: DppNet uses inhibitive attention to generate diverse DPP-like subsets much faster while matching reported downstream DPP performance.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models the distribution of total returns rather than only their average. A practical challenge is representing that distribution accurately with a finite model. The paper focuses on quantiles, which connect positions along a probability axis to the corresponding possible return values.

Earlier approaches learn either the probability side or the return-value side while keeping the other uniformly fixed or randomly sampled. The proposed fully parameterized quantile function learns both. A fraction proposal network generates a discrete collection of quantile fractions, and a quantile value network predicts their corresponding returns. Joint training seeks a better approximation of the underlying continuous distribution.

Experiments on 55 Atari games show significant improvements over existing distributional reinforcement learning algorithms. The paper also reports a new Atari Learning Environment record for non-distributed agents. These results support learning where to place quantile fractions as well as learning their values, giving the representation additional flexibility in the evaluated reinforcement learning setting.
neurips-2019-fully-parameterized-quantil.tldr: Jointly learning quantile fractions and return values improves distributional reinforcement learning performance on 55 Atari games.

paragraphs: Designing a protein for a desired three-dimensional structure requires reasoning about the relationship between its sequence and its shape. This inverse folding problem is difficult because sequence positions interact in complex ways. The paper develops generative models that use the target structure directly when designing protein sequences.

The approach represents the target structure as a graph and conditions relational language models on that graph. Its focus is on dependencies between positions that are far apart along the sequence but close together in three-dimensional space. Making those spatial relationships explicit gives the model a way to capture interactions that a sequence description alone does not express directly.

The authors report significant improvements in speed and robustness over both conventional and deep-learning-based methods for structure-based sequence design. The stated advance concerns the design process: generating sequences in relation to a specified structure more efficiently and robustly. They frame this as progress toward rapid, targeted biomolecular design using deep generative models.
neurips-2019-generative-models-for-graph.tldr: Graph-conditioned generative models exploit three-dimensional protein relationships to improve the speed and robustness of structure-based sequence design.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can be difficult to deploy on devices with limited computation and memory. Pruning addresses this by removing parameters while tolerating some loss in performance. This paper proposes a momentum-SGD-based method that performs pruning during training, using a compression target for the network as a whole.

At each training iteration, the method divides parameters into two groups and applies different update rules. Parameters treated as redundant receive ordinary weight decay without gradients from the task objective, gradually driving them toward zero. The global compression target allows the method to determine how sparsity is distributed across layers automatically.

The authors describe an end-to-end procedure that avoids manually tuning each layer's sparsity and does not require a separate, time-consuming retraining stage after pruning. They also report a stronger ability to find winning tickets: sparse subnetworks associated with favorable initialization. The contribution brings parameter removal into the optimization process itself, reducing the separate decisions and training stages needed for compression.
neurips-2019-global-sparse-momentum-sgd-.tldr: A momentum-SGD pruning method meets a global compression target during training by applying weight decay alone to redundant parameters.

paragraphs: An over-parameterized model can have many parameter settings that fit the training data perfectly. The optimization algorithm and its hyperparameters can influence which solution training reaches. This paper studies that influence as implicit regularization: a preference introduced by the training procedure even without an explicit penalty in the objective.

The analysis concerns discrete gradient updates for a two-layer linear network trained with least-squares loss. Using a rescaling of time, the authors show that training sequentially learns reduced-rank regression solutions whose rank gradually increases. In this description, the training trajectory moves through solutions of increasing rank rather than treating every possible solution equally.

The result requires initialization that vanishes and a sufficiently small step size. Those conditions are central to the stated characterization. Within that setting, the work makes optimization's bias concrete: the dynamics organize learning according to rank. This provides a precise example of how training choices can shape the solutions learned by an over-parameterized model.
neurips-2019-implicit-regularization-of-.tldr: Under vanishing initialization and small steps, a two-layer linear network learns reduced-rank regression solutions in increasing rank order.

paragraphs: Images arise from three-dimensional geometry interacting with light, but many image models do not explicitly account for that process. Incorporating rendering into learning is difficult because rasterization includes discrete assignments that interrupt gradient computation. This paper introduces DIB-Render to make image formation accessible to gradient-based training.

The key idea is to treat rasterization as weighted interpolation. That formulation permits analytical gradients and allows image-based learning signals to pass through several standard vertex shaders. The framework supports optimization of vertex positions, colors, normals, lighting directions, and texture coordinates, and can incorporate established lighting models from computer graphics.

The authors demonstrate single-image prediction of three-dimensional objects and generation of textured three-dimensional objects, training both applications exclusively with two-dimensional supervision. The result shows how image evidence can guide learning of three-dimensional content through a differentiable rendering process. The broader suggestion that understanding image formation may improve generalization remains a motivation, while the demonstrated contribution is the rendering framework and these two applications.
neurips-2019-learning-to-predict-3d-obje.tldr: DIB-Render makes rendering differentiable through weighted interpolation, enabling 3D object learning with exclusively 2D supervision.

paragraphs: The Sinkhorn distance is an entropy-regularized variant of Wasserstein distance used in machine learning and statistical inference. Standard computation becomes expensive because both memory and time requirements grow quadratically with dataset size. This paper addresses that scaling barrier with an approximation that combines the Nyström method and Sinkhorn scaling.

The authors prove that the combination produces an accurate approximation while requiring substantially less time and memory than other approaches. Their analysis examines both the Nyström method and the stability of Sinkhorn scaling. The stability component matters because an approximate computation must still lead to a reliable estimate of the final distance.

Experiments show that the method computes Sinkhorn distances on datasets hundreds of times larger than those handled by competing techniques. The contribution therefore links an approximation guarantee with a large practical expansion in manageable data size. It offers a way to retain accurate distance estimation when the resource requirements of standard computation would make the calculation impractical.
neurips-2019-massively-scalable-sinkhorn.tldr: Combining Nyström approximation with Sinkhorn scaling yields provably accurate distances and supports datasets hundreds of times larger in experiments.

paragraphs: The supplied abstract is a revision summary that identifies the method's central objective: learning representations that support fast adaptation while also minimizing interference. In the continual-learning setting named by the paper, these goals address how a representation supports new learning and how that learning interacts with other learned behavior.

The authors add a MAML-Rep baseline to test whether their objective improves on a MAML-like approach that also learns representations. They report noticeably better performance for their method. This comparison is relevant because both approaches learn representations, while the proposed objective explicitly includes interference reduction alongside rapid adaptation.

The revision also adds mini-ImageNet experiments, which the authors present as evidence that the method scales to more complex datasets. Algorithm pseudocode and a comparison with MAML clarify the approach, while terminology changes distinguish meta-training from a separate pretraining baseline and rename evaluation as meta-testing. These changes make the reported comparison and training stages easier to interpret.
neurips-2019-meta-learning-representatio.tldr: The revision reports that jointly targeting fast adaptation and reduced interference outperforms MAML-Rep and extends evaluation to mini-ImageNet.

paragraphs: Automated programming graders often tell students which tests failed, but that feedback may give little guidance about where to look in the code. NeuralBugLocator addresses this gap by identifying likely bug locations relative to a failing test. Its localization procedure does not require running the program.

The method first trains a tree convolutional neural network to predict whether a program passes or fails a particular test. It then applies neural prediction attribution to the trained model, examining which program lines contribute to the predicted outcome. This connects a model's correctness prediction to a location-based explanation that can help focus debugging.

Experiments show that NeuralBugLocator is generally more accurate than two program-spectrum baselines and one baseline based on syntactic differences. The finding concerns the accuracy of locating bugs, with the qualification that the advantage is general rather than universal. The practical contribution is to turn predicted test behavior into more targeted feedback than a failing-test report alone provides.
neurips-2019-neural-attribution-for-sema.tldr: NeuralBugLocator attributes predicted test outcomes to program lines to locate bugs without executing the program.

paragraphs: Features from object-classification networks can predict visually driven brain activity, but classification is too broad a task to make specific interpretations straightforward. This paper compares representations learned from 21 computer vision tasks to obtain a more task-specific view of visual processing in the brain.

The authors build encoding models that predict brain responses in BOLD5000, an fMRI dataset collected while people viewed more than 5,000 naturalistic images. Different task features predict activity in different brain regions. Features from three-dimensional tasks, including keypoint and edge detection, explain more variance than features from two-dimensional tasks, with this pattern observed across the whole brain.

The researchers construct a task graph from the spatial arrangement of brain areas well predicted by each representation. Comparing it with task relationships based on transfer-learning accuracy shows that more transferable tasks make similar predictions of brain responses. These predictive relationships provide evidence about task-specific organization in the human visual system and connect that organization with relationships among computer vision representations.
neurips-2019-neural-taskonomy-inferring-.tldr: Representations from 21 vision tasks reveal relationships between brain-response prediction, task transferability, and visual-system organization.

paragraphs: Hypothesis testing concerns deciding which explanation is supported by observations. In adversarial classification, that decision occurs in the presence of another participant with strategic interests. This paper studies nonzero-sum versions of such games, where the participants' objectives need not be exact opposites, under both Bayesian and Neyman–Pearson formulations.

The authors first establish the existence of mixed-strategy Nash equilibria. These are stable combinations of potentially randomized strategies, in which neither participant gains by changing strategy alone. They then investigate concentration phenomena associated with those equilibria, examining structure in the strategic behavior rather than only proving that equilibria exist.

The main results characterize exponential rates of convergence for classification errors at equilibrium. They parallel classical error-exponent results associated with the Chernoff–Stein lemma and Chernoff information, but use parameters determined by the adversarial model. Numerical experiments validate the results. The contribution connects strategic classification with precise descriptions of how its error behavior compares structurally with classical binary testing.
neurips-2019-nonzero-sum-adversarial-hyp.tldr: The paper establishes equilibria and characterizes classification-error exponents for nonzero-sum adversarial hypothesis-testing games.

paragraphs: Agents trained to cooperate with copies of themselves may develop coordination habits that people do not share. This paper investigates whether learning about human behavior helps address that mismatch. The authors introduce an Overcooked-inspired environment that demands coordination and train a simple model to imitate human play.

Agents trained through self-play or population-based training coordinate very well with themselves. When paired with the human model, however, they perform significantly worse than agents designed to cooperate with that model. This separates success with familiar artificial partners from success with a partner whose behavior reflects human play.

A planning experiment supports the same conclusion only when the human-aware planner receives the exact human model it faces. A study with real people shows a similar but weaker pattern. Qualitative observations attribute the gains to agents adapting to human gameplay. The findings therefore support incorporating human behavior into coordination training, while showing that the strength of the benefit depends on the evaluation and partner-model match.
neurips-2019-on-the-utility-of-learning-.tldr: Agents trained with a human behavior model coordinate better with that model, with a weaker corresponding benefit observed with real people.

paragraphs: The paper develops a quantum version of Wasserstein generative adversarial networks to improve adversarial training of quantum generative models. Its starting point is a proposed Wasserstein semimetric for quantum data. This measure inherits several theoretical benefits of its classical counterpart and provides the basis for the training design.

The authors explain how to turn the semimetric into quantum WGANs that can be implemented efficiently on quantum machines. Numerical studies using classical simulations of quantum systems show more robust and scalable performance than other quantum GAN proposals. The work also describes robustness in the presence of noisy quantum hardware as part of the approach's motivation and claimed benefits.

One application generates a roughly 50-gate, three-qubit circuit that closely approximates a three-qubit, one-dimensional Hamiltonian simulation circuit requiring more than 10,000 gates with standard techniques. This is a specific approximation result illustrating the method's potential for compact circuit generation. The reported numerical comparisons come from classical simulation of quantum systems.
neurips-2019-quantum-wasserstein-generat.tldr: A quantum Wasserstein training framework improves simulated quantum GAN performance and demonstrates a compact approximation of a much larger quantum circuit.

paragraphs: Recurrent spiking neural networks can process information across space and time and suit energy-efficient, event-driven hardware. Training them is difficult, however. Existing backpropagation approaches face costly temporal unrolling, unstable gradients, and the challenge of differentiating discontinuous spikes. This paper introduces ST-RSBP as a supervised training method for deep recurrent spiking networks.

The algorithm computes gradients of a rate-coded loss at the network output with respect to trainable parameters. Its central computation operates at the spike-train level, capturing temporal effects during both forward and backward passes. The authors attribute scalability to this formulation and describe support for networks with one recurrent layer or multiple feed-forward and recurrent layers.

Evaluations use speech and image datasets including TI46, N-TIDIGITS, Fashion-MNIST, and MNIST. The paper reports accuracy exceeding contemporary spiking backpropagation methods and conventional non-spiking deep learning models in these evaluations. The contribution is a training formulation that connects a defined output loss to parameter updates while retaining the temporal effects important to spiking computation.
neurips-2019-spike-train-level-backpropa.tldr: ST-RSBP trains recurrent spiking networks through spike-train-level gradients and reports strong accuracy on speech and image datasets.

paragraphs: Pipeline parallel learning distributes a network's computation across layers rather than across training examples. This paper investigates how quickly optimization can proceed in that arrangement. For smooth convex and non-convex objectives, it provides matching upper and lower complexity bounds and identifies a naive pipeline parallelization of Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent as optimal.

For non-smooth convex objectives, the authors introduce Pipeline Parallel Random Smoothing, or PPRS. Its convergence rate is within a factor of d to the one-quarter power of optimal, where d is the problem dimension. The overall accuracy dependence remains proportional to inverse squared error tolerance, but the depth-dependent component accelerates, giving near-linear speed-up and only slight dependence on network depth.

The paper separately studies non-smooth, non-convex problems empirically. On difficult, highly non-smooth problems with limited samples, including few-shot or adversarial learning settings, PPRS outperforms gradient descent and Nesterov's method. These experimental findings extend the practical investigation beyond the setting of the non-smooth convex guarantee.
neurips-2019-theoretical-limits-of-pipel.tldr: The paper establishes pipeline optimization limits and introduces random smoothing that accelerates depth-dependent computation for non-smooth convex objectives.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling makes sequential decisions using a posterior distribution, but computing that posterior often requires approximation. This paper asks whether an approximation that looks statistically close is necessarily good enough for decision-making. It studies the issue in bandit problems with a fixed number of available actions.

The authors show that even small constant error measured by alpha-divergence can produce linear regret, meaning cumulative lost reward can grow proportionally with the number of decisions. Approximation can cause insufficient exploration when alpha is below one or excessive exploration when alpha is above zero. These ranges overlap, so both kinds of failure are relevant for some divergence choices.

For positive alpha, the poor-performance possibility is described as unavoidable. For nonpositive alpha, adding a small amount of forced exploration can improve regret even with large constant inference error. The result shows why posterior approximation quality must be considered together with its effect on action selection: a small divergence error alone need not ensure effective exploration.
neurips-2019-thompson-sampling-and-appro.tldr: Small posterior approximation errors can cause linear regret in Thompson sampling, while forced exploration helps for nonpositive alpha-divergence settings.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation represents a matrix using a simpler structure while limiting reconstruction error. Column subset selection approaches build approximations from selected columns of the original matrix. This paper asks which entrywise error functions support approximation algorithms, extending the question beyond familiar sums of absolute or powered absolute errors.

The authors provide approximation algorithms for every error function satisfying approximate monotonicity and an approximate triangle inequality, and show that both conditions are necessary in their setting. Computational efficiency has an additional requirement: the error function must admit an efficient approximate regression algorithm. This distinguishes the structural conditions for approximation from the condition needed for efficient implementation.

The framework includes losses such as Huber loss that are not scale-invariant. The paper shows that this distinction changes column-selection structure: a factor of square root of log n more columns can be required than for standard l-p norms. Despite that obstacle, it provides the first efficient column subset selection algorithms for such error measures.
neurips-2019-towards-a-zero-one-law-for-.tldr: The paper characterizes error-function conditions for column subset approximation and extends efficient methods to non-scale-invariant losses such as Huber loss.
